image_description:
## 1) Chart type
- **Thematic geographic map** of the United States with **arrow glyphs** plotted by county.

## 2) Layout techniques
- Uses a **map-based spatial layout** (counties positioned by geographic location).
- No faceting or small multiples.
- Not stacked.
- Repeated **glyphs (arrows)** encode county-level values across the map.

## 3) Data variables

| Data Variable | Type of Variable | Visual Encoding |
|---|---|---|
| County | Categorical/nominal | One arrow per county; geographic position on the map |
| Geographic location | Spatial | Position on the U.S. map |
| Direction of change in population share | Categorical/nominal | Arrow direction/orientation (up-right vs up-left as shown in legend) |
| Magnitude of percentage-point change in share | Quantitative | Arrow length/size |
| Population group whose share increased (white vs people of color) | Categorical/nominal | Arrow color/hue (red for white, teal for people of color) |
| State name/abbreviation | Categorical/nominal | Text labels |
| City name | Categorical/nominal | Text labels |

Notes visible in the graphic indicate arrows represent **percentage-point change in share** and that counties with changes below one percentage point are not shown.

I also wonder why these areas are increasing. Are cities that have been historically POC-heavy decreasing in POC as they move to populate other locations in the US? Is the number of immigrants from non-European countries skyrocketing and sticking strictly to the east coast?

comments.raw_comment:
I notice that overall from 2010 to 2020 the share of people of color has increased significantly, with the growth experienced overtaking that of the white population by manyfold.  In particular, there has been a lot of growth in the POC population in the midwest and the east. The blue arrows are most concentrated around large cities on the map. Additionally, counties with longer arrows, or more growth, are concentrated around cities also. While growth in POC can be seen across the entire map, that of the white population is limited to a few areas. Mainly, the share of the white population in the southeast. 

To start, I wonder what is prompting the substantial growth in the POC population. Besides the concentration of this growth around large cities, I am intrigued by how evenly this growth is distributed in other parts of the map in the Midwest and the east coast. On the other hand, I wonder why there is far less growth in the western part of the United, especially California which I believe has one of the highest if not the highest minority populations in the U.S.

This relates to me and my community as an Asian American living in a white-dominated area. It is nice to visually see the significant increase in the POC population and process that the areas we live in are becoming more diverse. As the POC population increases, hopefully, that will parallel their representation and inclusion.

What direction has diversity in American been going in the past 10 years?

sections.label: notice
text: I notice that overall from 2010 to 2020 the share of people of color has increased significantly, with the growth experienced overtaking that of the white population by manyfold.  In particular, there has been a lot of growth in the POC population in the midwest and the east. The blue arrows are most concentrated around large cities on the map. Additionally, counties with longer arrows, or more growth, are concentrated around cities also. While growth in POC can be seen across the entire map, that of the white population is limited to a few areas. Mainly, the share of the white population in the southeast.

sections.label: wonder
text: To start, I wonder what is prompting the substantial growth in the POC population. Besides the concentration of this growth around large cities, I am intrigued by how evenly this growth is distributed in other parts of the map in the Midwest and the east coast. On the other hand, I wonder why there is far less growth in the western part of the United, especially California which I believe has one of the highest if not the highest minority populations in the U.S.

sections.label: relate
text: This relates to me and my community as an Asian American living in a white-dominated area. It is nice to visually see the significant increase in the POC population and process that the areas we live in are becoming more diverse. As the POC population increases, hopefully, that will parallel their representation and inclusion.

What do you notice?
- I think it's easy to focus on where most of the population growth is concentrated, the eastern US. I find it just as interesting that the west seems to have remained more or less the same in its racial makeup.

What do you wonder?
- Why does it seem that communities on the east coast are becoming more diverse than in the west? Even in the parts of CA with cities, the population growth of POC is far less prominent than on the east coast. It's not a political thing necessarily. There seems to be large population growth in both blue states like NJ or NY and red states like TN or KY. It begs the question: why? 

How does this relate to you and your community?
- Though I attend college in upstate NY, my hometown is in northern NJ. I come from a pretty racially/ethnically diverse community, and this map seems to reflect that quite well. I feel that as I've grown older my hometown has only gotten more and more diverse. I wonder if it has to do with our proximity to NYC, too, since there's a number of people in my community that commute by train. I'm unsure if this has anything to do with it, though.

comments.raw_comment:
A Political Presence in Population Rates-

In this graph, the first most noticeable feature is the major increase in people of color population rate and the lack thereof in the white population. The east side of the country is dominating in population rate compared to the west... but why? Well, the majority of major population increases happen in big cities such as Atlanta and Nashville. I found this interesting, given the location of these states on the map. It seems that the most population growth that happens in southern states is in the white population, and people of color population growth takes place everywhere else. Politics seem to play a major role in separating the population growth between people of color and the white community, given that the south tends to be more conservative. I wonder in this graph why the people of color population growth is so prevalent in northern California than in southern California.

The east side of the country is dominating in population rate compared to the west... but why? Well, the majority of major population increases happen in big cities such as Atlanta and Nashville. I found this interesting, given the location of these states on the map. It seems that the most population growth that happens in southern states is in the white population, and people of color population growth takes place everywhere else. Politics seem to play a major role in separating the population growth between people of color and the white community, given that the south tends to be more conservative.

I think it is interesting because Los Angeles is always perceived as the best place to be however, it doesn't seem like many new people are moving there.

This graph obviously shows that the population of the colored community has increased significantly in ALL areas, especially in the North. With that being said, it sort of encourages the idea of increasing your family, without putting thought into it, to receive more government aid.  That would be an interesting concept to explore amongst those who were eligible for aid during the peak of the pandemic.

comments.raw_comment: This graph was particularly interesting in the information it revealed. I noticed right away the large prevalence of blue arrows over red ones. In just about every location in the U.S., the share of people of color has increased. This is especially true in the eastern half of the country where the density of blue arrows is greater. Cities like Atlanta and New York City also seem to be filled with blue. The only areas where the share of the white population increased was dotted in places around Texas, South Carolina, Georgia, and a little bit of Louisiana. I wonder what the primary cause of this is. Is it because of immigration? Is it because of a difference in birth rates among different racial populations? Is it because of different groups of people moving across the country to different places? I live in Illinois, one of the places shown to have increasing diversity in the graph as evidenced by the density of arrows. It affects me, because I see a diverse group of people around me in my day to day life. In my opinion, it has caused me to be more aware of the various types of people and cultures that exist. A potential title for this graph, perhaps a bit dramatic but descriptive nonetheless, may be, “America, the melting pot of cultures”.

sections.label: notice
text: This graph was particularly interesting in the information it revealed. I noticed right away the large prevalence of blue arrows over red ones. In just about every location in the U.S., the share of people of color has increased. This is especially true in the eastern half of the country where the density of blue arrows is greater. Cities like Atlanta and New York City also seem to be filled with blue. The only areas where the share of the white population increased was dotted in places around Texas, South Carolina, Georgia, and a little bit of Louisiana.

comments.raw_comment: After studying the map, I noticed that not only did the POC population increase tremendously but ratio of the POC to the white population was a large amount. With a few outlier states such as South Carolina, most of the states included only arrows indicating POC population increase. Especially in the upper Midwest areas such as Illinois, Michigan, and Indiana. After investigating,  I wondered why the ratio of arrows was so different. I also wondered if it had anything to do with politics and the overall political views of each state. I also wondered if it had anything to do with the recent growth in immigration. This can relate to me and my community because the population as a whole country is changing. It was not necessarily one state that stood out the most but rather the entire country itself. A headline for this graph could be “minority populations on the rise all across America.”

comments.raw_comment: This exquisite graph grabbed my attention right away. The very first thing I noticed was the vast difference in the increase of people of color in the east than the west. I also notice major hotspots such as Atlanta and NYC where it seems these people of color are gathering. This graph makes it hard not to wonder, why is there such a drastic number of people of color vs white. You would think they would be similar or almost equal. This hypothesis is proved completely wrong by this graph. I would assume these results are due to interracial marriages, and more pull to the USA from other foreign countries that are declining. For example most white people come from Europe where it is easy to make a living. Where as colored people could be from third world countries who would do anything to get the chance to come to America. I personally come from an Indian decent and can see how this makes sense. For example my cousin in India is looking to go to college here in the US. She would be one of these arrows on this map. The opportunities here in the US are far greater and better than any other country. A good name for this graph could be, “A Colorful Nation.” Hinting at the amount of colored people immigrating to the US.

text: This exquisite graph grabbed my attention right away. The very first thing I noticed was the vast difference in the increase of people of color in the east than the west. I also notice major hotspots such as Atlanta and NYC where it seems these people of color are gathering.

I would assume these results are due to interracial marriages, and more pull to the USA from other foreign countries that are declining. For example most white people come from Europe where it is easy to make a living. Where as colored people could be from third world countries who would do anything to get the chance to come to America.

sections.label: relate
text: I personally come from an Indian decent and can see how this makes sense. For example my cousin in India is looking to go to college here in the US. She would be one of these arrows on this map. The opportunities here in the US are far greater and better than any other country.

text: A good name for this graph could be, “A Colorful Nation.” Hinting at the amount of colored people immigrating to the US.

comments.raw_comment: I noticed that from 2010 to 2020, the majority of counties in the United States had an increase in population for people of color, rather than white people. I also noticed that the population increases per county were mainly occurring in the East, and in the West population increases weren't as great. I also saw that there were hardly any population increases in the Southwest like, New Mexico, Arizona, and Nevada. I wonder why the population of people in color increased in the East, but not as much as the West. Is it maybe because there are less jobs/educational programs in the West, or are there more opportunities in the East? I also wonder why the Southwest has a significantly less population increase than any other area in the country. This relates to me because in this map, I live in Illinois and it is right in the middle of the huge population increase zone. I do know that there are a lot of jobs in Illinois especially Chicago, so maybe that is why more people decide to come to areas like Chicago and in the East. My dad works in Chicago, and it is always really busy with businesses and there are many opportunities for incomers. This graph really does show us how there can be almost favorites for where people of color like to live, and I wonder why it is more popular for people of color to choose the East rather than the West. A catchy title for this could be, "Is the West not the best?"

comments.raw_comment: I noticed in this graph that obviously, in a vast majority of places the POC population increased more than the non-hispanic white population did, often significantly so. There was one cluster of tracts in the southeastern coastal states that saw an increase to the contrary, with white growth exceeding that of POC, as well as a few outliers scattered around the country seemingly at random. It makes me wonder as to what could be the cause of that clustering of data in the southeast that went against the trend. Perhaps certain immigration trends there, or simply an existing population makeup that is overwhelmingly white. I’m also curious about what are likely the long term effects of this trend, politically and socially. Mostly, I hypothesize that the change that is occurring and that will likely continue to occur is generally positive. From what this graph shows, in some time the voter bases in most places will be composed of significantly more POC, although obviously some delay from the census is likely. Maybe minorities becoming a somewhat larger component of the population will help speed along social and political reforms for some of society’s race related issues, such as institutional racism in police departments that there has been such a huge movement to fix lately. Certainly even in my own community I can catch a glimpse of some of these issues, and the reform movements that come along with them. “Colored population swell brings hope for future reforms”

sections.label: notice
text: I noticed in this graph that obviously, in a vast majority of places the POC population increased more than the non-hispanic white population did, often significantly so. There was one cluster of tracts in the southeastern coastal states that saw an increase to the contrary, with white growth exceeding that of POC, as well as a few outliers scattered around the country seemingly at random.

sections.label: wonder
text: It makes me wonder as to what could be the cause of that clustering of data in the southeast that went against the trend. Perhaps certain immigration trends there, or simply an existing population makeup that is overwhelmingly white. I’m also curious about what are likely the long term effects of this trend, politically and socially.

sections.label: unprompted
text: Mostly, I hypothesize that the change that is occurring and that will likely continue to occur is generally positive. From what this graph shows, in some time the voter bases in most places will be composed of significantly more POC, although obviously some delay from the census is likely. Maybe minorities becoming a somewhat larger component of the population will help speed along social and political reforms for some of society’s race related issues, such as institutional racism in police departments that there has been such a huge movement to fix lately.

sections.label: relate

comments.raw_comment: The graph is a map that is showing arrows in different colors to symbolize the growth either in the share of POC or White Americans. One thing about the map that was truly interesting to me was the amount of green arrows that populated the area east of the Mississippi. In addition, I noticed how the POC growth was very concentrated in the area around Tennessee, Kentucky, and Georgia. I wonder why that is? I also ponder about why the ethnic makeup of cities especially on the west coast has less change than the more rural areas of the country. This data is relevant to my community as living in a nation of different races and ethnicities, it is important to understand how racial and ethnicity impact our society. This also relates to me personally as a person of color due to the fact that I have seen the raise of my own immigrant community in my community. I feel that a catchy title for this graph would be: Minority America on The Rise.

comments.raw_comment:
As apparently obvious by the sea of green arrows, the American population is becoming generally more diverse. However, some red arrows display that the share of the white population has increased; These red arrows are mostly spread out and oftentimes are due simply to chance. One may notice, though, that The Texas-Mexico border is drastically increasing their white population, and parts of South Carolina & Georgia too. Don’t be mistaken by the graph’s design, there are many smaller counties in the Eastern states compared to the Western states. This could potentially convey a wrong message that the West has barely been supporting diversity because the East is covered in many more green arrows. I also think that the designer’s choice of green being an increase in PoC per capita and red is an increase in white population per capita shows their stance on diversity. 

One of the main outliers in the widespread increase in diversity is the Texas-Mexico border. I wonder why their share of the white population has increased. We should also take into account the Census’ way of measuring these groups, how these definitions changed, and the graph designer’s choice to only measure White vs. PoC changes. Due to the county's proximity to Mexico, it’s interesting that there are more non-Hispanic whites. Perhaps people who have identified as Latino rather than Non-Hispanic white have entered those neighborhoods? (1/2)

I have noticed that there has been widespread increase in the population of people of color throughout the United States. While there are only a few exceptions in souther/southeastern areas like Georgia, South Carolina, Virginia and Texas. However, there are some interesting outliers, like a tract in Idaho and a tract in Michigan.

I wonder, what is the cause of these outliers? Are they politically, socially, or environmentally based? Furthermore, what is the cause of the 4 tracts across Colorado and New Mexico? What is the reasoning (that is common between two different states) that caused a net increase in the white population in these two tracts?

This relates to my and my community as we can understand where we as a country are headed in terms of acceptance. We are becoming a more nationally diverse country, with people of all races living all across the country.

This graph visualizes the diversification of the United States in a very unique way. A way that on paper you might think would create a very "busy" graph, but really demonstrates how all these little areas can paint an enormous picture when it comes to the nation as a whole. A catchy title for this graph might be "The Wave of Color Washing over the United States"

comments.raw_comment:
I noticed most places in the United States had an increased share of people of color. The majority of the places that had an increased share of white people was in the South. States like Virginia, North Carolina, South Carolina, Georgia, and other southern states all had a portion that increased the shard of white people. I also noticed the arrow density was much more clustered in the East side of the country, in the Midwest and New England. This means that that area has changed much more in diversity than places in the west like Wyoming. 

I wonder why this change is happening, what are the causes to this change that seems fairly steady across the whole country. Is it that people of color that were once highly concentrated in certain areas are spreading out? Is it that there are more people of color due to more mixed people and immigrants? I wonder what the explanation is for this fairly universal increase in share of colored people. 

This relates to my community because it shows the share of people of color is most likely going up in my community. It means the community is becoming more diverse, and America seems to be becoming more diverse as a whole. 

This graph demonstrates the increase of share of people of color, or diversity, or of the untied states relative to the location. It shows overall that diversity has gone up since 2010. A catchy headline would be - “Diversity Over 10 Years - How Has It Changed?”

This pattern occurs specifically along the South Eastern coast. On the East coast, the trend begins in Maryland, continuing down southwards through Virginia, the Carolinas, and Florida. I think a possible explanation for this pattern is that these states may have areas with predominantly white communities, pr  are possibly more isolated, resulting in an increase of white populations. This information is relevant to my community because racial diversity has the potential to enrich our culture as a whole, providing, among other things, a wider range of values and ideas. I would caption this graph “Region v. Race: A Closer Look at Diversity in America Today”

comments.raw_comment:
Thanks to all students who responded during this shortened school week.   Here are some of the catchy headlines that we received: “Rising Diversity Rates in America: The Melting Pot” by Lauren of Pennsylvania, “Are Minorities Becoming the Majority?” by Allie of Gladeville Middle School in Mount Juliet, Tennessee, and “Cultural Equilibrium: America’s Diverse Outlook” by Andrew from Illinois.

You can continue to post responses.  Please check back by Friday, Jan. 21 to see the Reveal with a link to the original New York Times article, some questions about the graph, and a Stat Nugget.

Please visit our archive to see all graphs in this series (tinyurl.com/NYTGraphs).

Signing off – Sharon Hessney from Boston, Massachusetts, which had an 8.5 percent increase in people of color* over the past decade, and George Carr of Greenville, South Carolina, whose county of Greenville had a 5.9% percent increase.

text:
Thanks to all students who responded during this shortened school week.   Here are some of the catchy headlines that we received: “Rising Diversity Rates in America: The Melting Pot” by Lauren of Pennsylvania, “Are Minorities Becoming the Majority?” by Allie of Gladeville Middle School in Mount Juliet, Tennessee, and “Cultural Equilibrium: America’s Diverse Outlook” by Andrew from Illinois.

You can continue to post responses.  Please check back by Friday, Jan. 21 to see the Reveal with a link to the original New York Times article, some questions about the graph, and a Stat Nugget.

comments.raw_comment: Something I notice that the diversity of the east side of the United States has a far greater increase than the west side, and that there are large growths in northern Georgia, Maryland and New Jersey as well. Something I wonder is why there is so much growth in people of color with respect to the white population. I would think that whites and non-whites would have similar rates of growth, but the graph clearly shows that there was a vast disparate increase in minority population when compared with whites in the past ten years. Of course I suppose these changes could be due to immigration and interracial marriages and multi-ethnic children. This graph directly relates to my family because my brother (non-white) was born in 2012 and so we personally contributed to the increase in diversity in Illinois. Also, from a cultural perspective, I believe that many specific cultural practices have become more widely accepted than in the past. I think a good name for this graph would be “Cultural Equilibrium: America’s Diverse Outlook” because this not only shows an equalization of races and cultures, but also predicts that this trend will continue to occur and America will soon be a hub of equality and diversity.

I'd assume it was due to the overall diversity of a state's population, but on the other hand, a state like Arkansas with predominantly white towns that are known to be extremely racist and hateful towards the BIPOC community have still experienced increases in people of color. I guess this would unfortunately lead to even more discrimination and hate toward BIPOC and other people of color.

3. Although the number of people of color in the U.S. has signifcantly increased over time (and still continues to increase), we still experience increasing rates of racism and discrimination. I am disgusted by the amount of racism and hate that is still prevalent in society, and will continue to emphasize the importance of advocating for change and social justice.

sections.label: notice
text: 1. I notice that the population of people of color has largely increased throughout a majority of the U.S. since 2010. This increase happens to be more prevalent on the eastern side of the U.S., while the western side still has increases, but much less.

sections.label: wonder
text: 2. I wonder why the POC population increases in some states more than others. I'd assume it was due to the overall diversity of a state's population, but on the other hand, a state like Arkansas with predominantly white towns that are known to be extremely racist and hateful towards the BIPOC community have still experienced increases in people of color. I guess this would unfortunately lead to even more discrimination and hate toward BIPOC and other people of color.

sections.label: relate
text: 3. Although the number of people of color in the U.S. has signifcantly increased over time (and still continues to increase), we still experience increasing rates of racism and discrimination. Specifically the BIPOC community experiences a disproportionate amount of racism, despite the diversifying population. I am disgusted by the amount of racism and hate that is still prevalent in society, and will continue to emphasize the importance of advocating for change and social justice.

sections.label: notice
text: I notice that each arrow represents a county. Red arrows are for an increase in white population, and green arrows are for an increase in the population of people of color. There is much more green that red on the map. The eastern half of the country has much more green arrows than the western half. The most red arrows are in states in the southern part of the east coast. Hawaii only has two arrows, a small green one and a larger red one.

sections.label: wonder
text: I wonder if it was immigration that caused the increase in population of people of color, or if it was mostly internal movement of people of color who already lived in the US. I wonder why there are so few red arrows and why those arrows are concentrated in a certain area. I wonder if Hawaii only has two counties, or if there are more counties that didn’t have a change greater than 1%.

comments.raw_comment:
Diversity Shifts in POC Populations in the U.S. over the Last Decade 

Right off the bat, I'm noticing that populations of people of color have crowded around the East Coast, the SouthEast, as well as Midwest. This implies that the populations of POC (people of color) have definitely increased; in other words, diversity throughout the U.S. has gone up. I find it interesting that changes in white populations on the other hand have stayed relatively the same in comparison. This makes me wonder about the different factors that may have influenced non-white communities to expand away from the western states. I also think it is interesting that states like Georgia, that have historically been largely populated with people of color, has started to see an equally amount of increases in white communities. I'm also thinking if there will be any negative impacts in the long run with more people crowding into a specific area of the U.S. (e.g. overpopulation in cities). 

These changes in diversity relates to my community when considering how the area I live in is populated with a large white population. The significant changes in diversity through out the East Coast makes me wonder how the population might change in my area in the next decade.

sections.label: notice
text: Right off the bat, I'm noticing that populations of people of color have crowded around the East Coast, the SouthEast, as well as Midwest. sections.label: wonder
text: This makes me wonder about the different factors that may have influenced non-white communities to expand away from the western states. I also think it is interesting that states like Georgia, that have historically been largely populated with people of color, has started to see an equally amount of increases in white communities. I'm also thinking if there will be any negative impacts in the long run with more people crowding into a specific area of the U.S. (e.g. overpopulation in cities).

sections.label: relate
